quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Airline attendants, receptionists, and call-center staff are often required to appear cheerful regardless of how they feel. Sociologists call the effort of producing an expected emotion 'emotional labor,' and they note that it is rarely counted in job descriptions or pay. Workers who can genuinely feel the emotion they are asked to display tend to cope better than those who merely act it, but customers can usually tell the difference, and the employer benefits when the feeling is real. The difficulty is that emotion cannot be commanded. Organizations that recognize this treat the work as a skill deserving training, rest, and the freedom to step away from abuse, rather than as a smile that costs nothing.
options: Customers Being Able to Detect Acted Emotions Easily
Pressures Facing Workers in Service Jobs
The Recognition That Emotional Labor Deserves
Sociologists Naming Unpaid Emotional Effort
quests.correctAnswer: The Recognition That Emotional Labor Deserves
quests.hint: The passage ends with a contrast between two ways of seeing the work. Which title carries that contrast's point?
quests.explanation: Service-job pressures is wider, customers' detection is one point, and the sociologists' term is only where the discussion starts. The passage argues that displaying feelings is real work that organizations should acknowledge and support.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title joins the concept, the difficulty of commanding emotion, and the closing argument for treating the work as a skill.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Humans have mapped the surface of Mars in greater detail than most of the ocean floor. The reason is not lack of interest but physics: light reaches Mars's surface through thin air, whereas seawater absorbs light and radio waves within meters, forcing researchers to rely on sound and slow ships. A single vessel might survey only a few hundred square kilometers a day, and the ocean covers most of the planet. Yet the ocean floor governs currents, shapes fisheries, and hides fault lines that produce earthquakes and tsunamis. Recent collaborative projects aim to complete the map within a decade, on the argument that knowing our own planet's terrain is a practical need, not a luxury.
options: Projects Aiming to Finish the Map Within a Decade
The Ocean Floor: Hard to Map, Important to Know
Why Sound and Ships Are Used Underwater
Comparing Earth's Terrain with Other Planets
quests.correctAnswer: The Ocean Floor: Hard to Map, Important to Know
quests.hint: The passage explains a difficulty and then argues a need. Which title includes both?
quests.explanation: The planet comparison is the opening hook, sound and ships explain the difficulty, and the decade-long projects are the response. The passage's full message is that the sea floor is hard to chart but worth charting.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice captures both why the ocean floor remains unmapped and why the passage says it matters.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: In many nineteenth-century homes, novels were read aloud in the evening, one person reading while others sewed or listened. Authors knew this and often published in installments, ending each with a question that families would discuss until the next number arrived. The habit shaped the writing itself: dialogue was vivid, scenes were clear enough to be heard, and chapters were built to be read in a sitting. The silent, private reading now taken for granted is comparatively recent, and it has changed what authors can do, allowing longer sentences and inward reflection that would exhaust a listener. Forms of reading, in short, are not neutral; they leave traces in the works written for them.
options: History of the Novel
Novels Published in Installments
How Reading Habits Shape Literature
How Silent Reading Allowed Longer Sentences
quests.correctAnswer: How Reading Habits Shape Literature
quests.hint: Look at how the final sentence generalizes from the examples. What is it about 'forms of reading'?
quests.explanation: The history of the novel is broader, and installments and longer sentences are two examples of the effect. The passage's claim is that the way a text is read shapes how it is written.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title states the general claim that the oral and silent habits of reading each influenced the books written for them.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: When a famous scientist and an unknown one publish similar work, the famous name usually receives most of the credit. Sociologists call this the Matthew effect, after a passage suggesting that those who have will be given more. Its consequences accumulate: recognition brings funding, funding brings better students and equipment, and these bring further discoveries, which reinforce the reputation. Talent and effort matter, but early advantages are magnified over time. The effect is not confined to science; it appears in art, business, and schooling. Recognizing it invites institutions to examine whether rewards flow to the best work or merely to the best-known names.
options: How Credit Flows Toward the Already Famous
Funding Following Recognition
Modern Science: The Role of Reputation
Institutions Examining How Rewards Are Given
quests.correctAnswer: How Credit Flows Toward the Already Famous
quests.hint: The passage moves from one example to a wider pattern to a question. Which title covers the pattern itself?
quests.explanation: Reputation in science is narrower than the passage's scope, funding is one step in the cycle, and the institutions' review is the closing suggestion. The passage describes how existing recognition draws further recognition.
quests.whyThisTitle: It names the pattern that the science example, the accumulating benefits, and the wider spread all illustrate.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Aviation's safety record owes much to a habit that seems counterintuitive: treating mistakes as information rather than as occasions for punishment. Pilots and controllers are encouraged to report errors and near-misses, often confidentially, and investigators focus on how the system allowed the error, not on who made it. The approach depends on trust; if reporting brought penalties, people would hide mistakes, and the industry would lose the very data it needs. Critics worry that it lets negligence go unpunished, and in cases of deliberate recklessness, the system does distinguish. But for ordinary human error, the evidence suggests that learning prevents more accidents than blame does.
options: Safety Built on Blame-Free Reporting
Confidential Reporting of Near-Misses
Reducing Accidents in Transportation
Critics Worried About Unpunished Negligence
quests.correctAnswer: Safety Built on Blame-Free Reporting
quests.hint: The last sentence states a comparison. What two approaches does it compare?
quests.explanation: Reducing accidents is broader, confidential reporting is one practice, and the critics' worry is an objection the passage answers. The whole passage explains why blame-free reporting has improved safety.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title captures the approach, the reasoning behind it, and its result.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Eyewitness testimony carries great weight in court, because jurors find a confident account persuasive. Yet decades of research show that memory reconstructs events rather than replaying them, and that confidence is only loosely related to accuracy. Suggestive questions can alter recollections, and a witness who sees a suspect in one lineup may later 'remember' that face from the crime. Some courts now instruct jurors about these limits and require that lineups be run by officers who do not know which person is the suspect. The reforms do not dismiss witnesses; they treat testimony as evidence to be handled with care, like any fragile material.
options: Jurors Finding Confident Witnesses Persuasive
Why Confident Eyewitnesses Need Careful Handling
The Reliability of Human Memory
Lineups Run by Officers Who Do Not Know the Suspect
quests.correctAnswer: Why Confident Eyewitnesses Need Careful Handling
quests.hint: Notice that the last sentence says what the reforms do and do not do. What is the balanced view?
quests.explanation: Human memory in general is wider, the lineup rule is one reform, and jurors' persuasion is the problem's starting point. The passage argues for handling testimony carefully without discarding it.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title reflects the balanced conclusion that testimony is valuable but fragile.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Loneliness is often treated as a private feeling, yet health researchers increasingly count it as a public concern. Studies link chronic loneliness with poorer sleep, higher blood pressure, and shorter lives, effects comparable to well-known risks. Because loneliness is not the same as being alone, remedies that merely add contact, such as a scheduled visit, may not help if the contact feels formal. Programs that bring people together around shared tasks, such as cooking or gardening, appear to work better, because the activity provides both a reason to meet and something to talk about. The finding suggests that connection is built less by attendance than by purpose.
options: Tackling Loneliness Through Shared Activity
Public Health and Modern Lifestyles
Loneliness Linked to Poorer Sleep and Blood Pressure
Why Being Alone Differs from Feeling Lonely
quests.correctAnswer: Tackling Loneliness Through Shared Activity
quests.hint: Look at how the last sentence contrasts 'attendance' with 'purpose.' What does that suggest about the remedy?
quests.explanation: Public health in general is broader, and the health links and the definition of loneliness are earlier points. The passage builds toward a remedy: shared activity gives contact a purpose.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice expresses the passage's conclusion about what works against loneliness, which the earlier points lead up to.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: When politicians ask what a research project will produce, scientists often struggle to answer. The most valuable discoveries frequently arise from curiosity with no evident use: the study of a bacterium's odd defense led to a gene-editing tool; work on the properties of quantum particles underlies modern electronics. Because such payoffs cannot be predicted, an economy that funds only research with a clear goal may choke off its own future breakthroughs. Yet it would be irresponsible to spend without accountability. A sensible balance funds many small exploratory projects, judges them by the quality of their questions rather than promised products, and accepts that most will not lead anywhere.
options: Accountability When Spending Public Money
A Bacterium's Defense Leading to Gene Editing
How Governments Decide Research Budgets
Defending Research with Unpredictable Uses
quests.correctAnswer: Defending Research with Unpredictable Uses
quests.hint: Ask what the passage argues for, and what limit it acknowledges.
quests.explanation: Budget decisions are the setting, the bacterium is one example, and accountability is the qualification the passage adds. The main claim is that unpredictable research deserves support, managed sensibly.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title captures the argument for funding open-ended research along with the balance the last sentences propose.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: A handbag that costs a year's wages is not, in practical terms, better than one at a fiftieth of the price, and the makers of luxury goods know this. Their products are valued for what they signal: that the owner can afford them, and that few others can. This explains a counterintuitive habit of the industry: rather than making more of a popular item when demand rises, luxury firms often raise the price or limit supply. Scarcity itself is part of what buyers are paying for. Attempts to expand into the mass market carry a risk, since the more common the product becomes, the less it says about the person carrying it.
options: Luxury Firms Limiting Supply
The Risk of Entering the Mass Market
Raising Prices When Demand Increases
Economics of Fashion and Luxury Retail
quests.correctAnswer: Luxury Firms Limiting Supply
quests.hint: The passage explains a 'counterintuitive habit.' What is the habit and what explains it?
quests.explanation: The economics of fashion is wider, and rising prices and mass-market risk are a practice and a consequence. The passage's core is why scarcity keeps luxury products valuable.
quests.whyThisTitle: It names the industry habit and the reason for it that ties the details together.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Many coastal towns fill in August and empty in February, leaving businesses to earn a year's income in a few crowded weeks. Some have tried to spread visitors through the year with winter festivals, cheaper off-season fares, and events that use the quiet months. Results are mixed: a festival can lift hotel bookings but strain a town that lacks staff in winter, and visitors drawn by low prices may spend less. Still, towns that succeed tend to build on what is distinctive about the off-season, such as storm watching or quiet walks, rather than imitating the summer. The most durable approach treats the empty months as a different product, not a failed version of the busy ones.
options: Winter Festivals Lifting Hotel Bookings
Building a Distinct Off-Season Instead of Copying Summer
Challenges of Coastal Tourism
Off-Season Visitors Who Spend Less
quests.correctAnswer: Building a Distinct Off-Season Instead of Copying Summer
quests.hint: The last sentence states what is most durable. What is it?
quests.explanation: Coastal tourism's challenges is the setting, and the festivals and low-spending visitors are mixed results. The passage's conclusion is that the quiet season works best when treated as its own offering.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title captures the passage's final recommendation and the mixed results that lead to it.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Asked whether they understand how a zipper works, most people say yes. Asked to write out the mechanism step by step, they discover gaps and lower their rating. Psychologists call this the illusion of explanatory depth: we mistake familiarity for understanding, since everyday objects and ideas are constantly at hand. The illusion appears in politics too, where people who rate their grasp of a policy highly often revise their confidence, and sometimes their views, after being asked to explain it in detail. Explanation, then, is not only communication but a test of one's own knowledge, revealing what the mind has been taking for granted.
options: Revising Views After Detailed Explanation
Explaining How a Zipper Works
How People Judge Their Own Knowledge
Using Explanation to Test Our Understanding
quests.correctAnswer: Using Explanation to Test Our Understanding
quests.hint: Notice that the last sentence says what explanation is 'not only.' What else is it?
quests.explanation: Self-judgment in general is wider, and the zipper and the revised views are two examples. The passage's key idea is that attempting to explain exposes gaps in what we think we know.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title states the idea that the zipper and policy examples both support.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Visitors to former battlefields, disaster sites, and prisons are sometimes accused of morbid curiosity. Researchers who interview them find more varied motives: a wish to honor victims, a desire to understand events that textbooks compress into a paragraph, or a family connection to the place. How a site presents itself matters. Those that invite reflection through quiet spaces and the voices of survivors tend to produce solemn visitors, while those that treat the site as entertainment attract behavior that offends. The same location can therefore become a place of memory or of spectacle, depending less on the visitors than on how the place shapes their attention.
options: Survivors' Voices in Quiet Spaces
Memory or Spectacle: How Sites of Tragedy Guide Visitors
Motives for Visiting Disaster Sites
Why People Travel to Historic Places
quests.correctAnswer: Memory or Spectacle: How Sites of Tragedy Guide Visitors
quests.hint: The passage says the outcome depends 'less on the visitors' than on something else. What?
quests.explanation: Reasons for travel are broader, and the survivors' voices and the visitors' motives are details in the argument. The last sentence brings out the main point: presentation shapes how visitors behave.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice expresses the claim that the site's presentation determines whether it becomes a place of memory or spectacle.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: We speak of the economy as if it were a machine that can be 'fine-tuned,' a living body that can 'overheat,' or a weather system that 'turns stormy.' Such metaphors are not decoration; each suggests different responses: machines are repaired, bodies healed, storms endured. Researchers have found that people's views on policies shift depending on which image they are given, even when the facts are identical. Because metaphors work quietly, it is easy to be steered without noticing. Awareness does not mean avoiding them, which would be impossible, but asking what a chosen image highlights and what it leaves out.
options: Noticing What Metaphors Highlight and Hide
Policy Views Shifting with Different Images
Figurative Language: Its Role in Speech
The Economy Described as a Machine
quests.correctAnswer: Noticing What Metaphors Highlight and Hide
quests.hint: The passage ends with what awareness 'does not mean' and what it does. What is the recommended habit?
quests.explanation: Figurative language in general is wider, the machine image is one example, and the shifting views are the evidence. The passage recommends asking what an image emphasizes and omits.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title captures the passage's recommended awareness and the effects it is meant to guard against.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: In many fields, a small share of causes produces a large share of effects: a fifth of customers may account for most sales, a few bugs for most crashes, a handful of habits for most of a person's progress. The pattern, often called the Pareto principle, is not an exact law, and the proportions vary. Its practical value is as a prompt to look for the vital few before spreading effort evenly. Yet the principle can mislead if taken too rigidly: the less visible items may be the ones that keep the system running, and neglecting them can bring the whole thing down. The skill lies in prioritizing without dismissing what supports the priorities.
options: A Fifth of Customers Producing Most Sales
Pareto Principle as an Inexact Rule
Ways to Manage Time and Effort
Focusing on the Vital Few Without Ignoring the Rest
quests.correctAnswer: Focusing on the Vital Few Without Ignoring the Rest
quests.hint: Look at the 'Yet' that begins the second half. How does it change the advice?
quests.explanation: Managing time is wider, and the customer example and the inexactness are supporting points. The passage recommends prioritizing while remembering that the lesser items may sustain the whole.
quests.whyThisTitle: It joins the advice to prioritize with the warning not to neglect what supports the priorities.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Reenactors who dress in period clothing and repeat old crafts often say they seek authenticity, yet they know it is out of reach. They cannot recreate the diseases, the fears, or the sense of not knowing how events would end. What they can do is test what the sources describe: how long it takes to march in wool, how heavy a musket feels after a day. These small discoveries correct assumptions that documents leave unstated. Historians do not treat such experiments as proof, but many find them useful as questions to bring back to the archives. Authenticity, in this sense, is less a destination than a method of asking better questions.
options: Ways Communities Celebrate the Past
Reenactment and the Method of Inquiry
Marching in Wool Clothing for a Day
Historians' Caution About Experimental Evidence
quests.correctAnswer: Reenactment and the Method of Inquiry
quests.hint: Look at how the final sentence redefines 'authenticity.' What does it become?
quests.explanation: Community celebration is a different framing, the wool march is one example, and the historians' caution is a qualification. The passage's central claim is that reenactment works as a way of raising questions.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title expresses the redefinition in the last sentence, which the examples and the historians' view support.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Economists have long puzzled over gifts: a cash payment would let recipients buy exactly what they want, yet people give objects that may be unwanted. Studies suggest that the gift's value lies partly in what it says about the giver's attention, and that recipients appreciate thoughtfulness more than givers expect. Givers, meanwhile, tend to choose gifts that will impress at the moment of unwrapping, whereas recipients prefer items that will prove useful for months. The mismatch suggests that the difficulty is not generosity but perspective: each side imagines the exchange from a different moment. Better gifts may come from asking what will be used, not what will surprise.
options: Recipients Valuing Thoughtfulness
Why Givers and Recipients Judge Gifts Differently
Cash Payments Compared with Objects
Gifts as Economic Puzzles
quests.correctAnswer: Why Givers and Recipients Judge Gifts Differently
quests.hint: The passage says the difficulty is 'not generosity but perspective.' What does that mean for the title?
quests.explanation: The economics of generosity is broader, cash versus objects is the puzzle at the start, and thoughtfulness is one finding. The passage's core is the difference in how givers and recipients view the exchange.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title names the mismatch of viewpoints that the studies and the closing advice revolve around.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: In several countries, rivers and forests have been granted legal standing, allowing guardians to sue on their behalf. Supporters argue that existing law treats nature as property, so harm to a river is actionable only when a person can show a personal loss. Granting rights, they say, matches the law to the facts: a river's health matters even when no individual can claim damage. Critics question how a river's 'wishes' can be known and whether the approach shifts decisions from voters to lawyers. Early cases suggest that the change matters less as a philosophical statement than as a practical way of ensuring someone is empowered to speak when harm occurs.
options: Critics Doubting That a River's Wishes Can Be Known
Guardians Suing on Behalf of Forests
How Law Protects the Environment
Legal Standing for Rivers and Who Speaks for Them
quests.correctAnswer: Legal Standing for Rivers and Who Speaks for Them
quests.hint: The final sentence assesses the change. What does it say matters most?
quests.explanation: Environmental law in general is wider, the critics' doubt is one side of the debate, and the guardians are the mechanism. The passage weighs arguments and concludes that the practical effect is having someone empowered to speak.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice covers the idea, the debate, and the practical value the passage emphasizes.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: In a rocky shore experiment, ecologists removed a single species, a starfish that preys on mussels. Within months, mussels overran the rock and crowded out most other species, and the diversity of the shore collapsed. The starfish was not the most abundant creature, yet its absence transformed everything. Ecologists coined the term 'keystone species' for such cases, where influence is far greater than numbers suggest. The concept has changed how conservation is planned: instead of protecting whatever is most numerous or most attractive, managers ask which species hold the community together.
options: Mussels Overrunning Rock Surfaces
Protecting Biodiversity on Rocky Shores
Conservation Focused on Attractive Species
Keystone Species and Influence
quests.correctAnswer: Keystone Species and Influence
quests.hint: Which title reflects the concept the experiment gave rise to?
quests.explanation: Protecting shore biodiversity is narrower in setting, the mussels are one effect, and attractive species are what conservation used to prioritize. The passage builds from an experiment to a concept and its practical impact.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title names the concept the experiment illustrates and its point about influence being unrelated to numbers.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Many traditions include periods of deliberate restraint: fasting from food, silence, or rest from work. Anthropologists note that these practices differ in details but share a structure: a limit voluntarily accepted for a time, followed by a return. Participants often describe the value not as deprivation but as heightened attention; ordinary meals or conversation seem richer afterward. Some secular versions have appeared, such as digital detox weekends, though critics say that without the shared meaning and community that traditions supply, they fade quickly. The comparison suggests that restraint works best when embedded in something larger than personal discipline.
options: Digital Detox Weekends Fading Quickly
Participants Describing Heightened Attention
Restraint Rooted in Shared Meaning
Religious and Cultural Traditions Around the World
quests.correctAnswer: Restraint Rooted in Shared Meaning
quests.hint: Notice that the last sentence draws a conclusion from a comparison. What is it?
quests.explanation: World traditions is wider, digital detox is the secular case, and heightened attention is the participants' report. The passage concludes that restraint is most effective within a shared framework.
quests.whyThisTitle: It expresses the closing conclusion that the traditional and secular examples support.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: In care homes, people with advanced dementia who no longer recognize relatives sometimes sing entire songs from their youth. Researchers think music is stored in ways that differ from other memories and remains reachable when they fade. Playlists tailored to a resident's past have been reported to reduce agitation and stimulate conversation, though controlled studies show modest effects, and music does not cure the disease. The lasting value seems to lie in connection: for a moment, the person is addressed as an individual with a history. The approach demands little equipment but real attention from carers.
options: Ways Care Homes Support Residents
Residents Singing Songs from Their Youth
Personal Music and Connection in Dementia Care
Modest Effects Shown in Controlled Studies
quests.correctAnswer: Personal Music and Connection in Dementia Care
quests.hint: The passage says where the 'lasting value' lies. What is it?
quests.explanation: Care home support is broader, the singing is the opening image, and the modest studies are a qualification. The passage's emphasis is on the connection music creates for each individual.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title reflects the value the passage identifies: connection with the person through music from their own past.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Holding back struggling students so that they repeat a year seems intuitive: more time should help them catch up. Large studies of grade repetition, however, find little lasting academic benefit, and suggest that repeaters are more likely to leave school early, perhaps because of stigma or discouragement. Schools that provide extra support inside the regular class, such as small tutoring groups, tend to do better at similar cost. The lesson is not that struggling students should be ignored but that the intuitive remedy can prove counterproductive. Programs need to be judged by results, not by how sensible they sound.
options: Small Tutoring Groups Inside Regular Classes
Helping Students Who Fall Behind
Repeating a Year Leading Students to Leave Early
Judging Remedies by Results
quests.correctAnswer: Judging Remedies by Results
quests.hint: Look at how the last sentence gives the general lesson. What is it, beyond grade repetition?
quests.explanation: Helping students is broader, tutoring is the alternative, and early dropout is the finding. The passage's lesson is about evaluating well-meant programs by their outcomes.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title captures the general lesson that grade repetition illustrates.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Popular stories emphasize young prodigies, yet studies of creative work find that major contributions appear across a range of ages, and that the pattern depends on the field. Mathematicians and poets often produce early breakthroughs, while historians and novelists tend to peak later, when their work depends on accumulated knowledge. There are also two styles within fields: some creators work through sudden, conceptual leaps and others through gradual experiment, and these styles peak at different times. The result is that creativity cannot be assigned to one stage of life. Institutions that offer opportunities only to the young risk missing contributions of a different, but no lesser, kind.
options: Nature of Creative Genius
Mathematicians and Poets Making Early Breakthroughs
Different Fields and Styles Peak at Different Ages
Institutions Favoring the Young
quests.correctAnswer: Different Fields and Styles Peak at Different Ages
quests.hint: The passage says creativity 'cannot be assigned to one stage of life.' What supports that?
quests.explanation: Creative genius in general is wider, early breakthroughs are one half of the evidence, and institutional favoritism is the implication. The main claim is about variety in when creative work appears.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice reflects the variation across fields and working styles that the passage uses to reject a single peak age.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Kintsugi is the Japanese practice of mending broken pottery with lacquer mixed with gold, so that the cracks become visible lines of beauty. The idea behind it differs from repair that hides damage: the break is treated as part of the object's history, not as a flaw to be concealed. Some craftspeople see in the practice a philosophy of acceptance, and psychologists have used it as a metaphor for recovering from setbacks. The metaphor has limits, since a broken bowl is not a broken life, and pain is not made valuable simply by being decorated. Its appeal lies in a modest suggestion: that what has been damaged need not be discarded or disguised.
options: Traditional Japanese Craft Techniques
Gold Lacquer Filling the Cracks
Psychologists Using Repair as a Metaphor
Visible Repair and the Value of Damage
quests.correctAnswer: Visible Repair and the Value of Damage
quests.hint: The passage describes a craft, then an idea, then its limits. Which title fits the whole?
quests.explanation: Japanese crafts is wider in kind, the gold lacquer is one detail, and the psychologists' use is one extension. The passage develops the idea that damage can be part of an object's history and value.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title covers the practice, the idea behind it, and the caution about its use as a metaphor.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Young children ask hundreds of questions a day, and adults often treat them as a phase to be endured. Researchers who have recorded these questions find that children do not simply want answers; they are testing what kinds of explanations are available, and they persist when the answer is vague. Children who receive real explanations, even simple ones, ask more questions and appear to learn faster than those who are brushed off. Parents do not need to know everything. Admitting ignorance, and finding out together, teaches something valuable: that questions are a way of thinking, not an interruption of it.
options: Parents Admitting What They Do Not Know
Children's Questions and Real Thinking
How Young Children Learn Language
Children Persisting When Answers Are Vague
quests.correctAnswer: Children's Questions and Real Thinking
quests.hint: The last sentence says what questions are not. What does the passage say they are?
quests.explanation: Language learning is a different subject, admitting ignorance is one piece of advice, and persistence is one finding. The passage argues that children's questions are a form of thought that deserves real responses.
quests.whyThisTitle: It captures the passage's view of questions as thinking and its advice to respond seriously.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: After a flood or earthquake, pressure to rebuild quickly is intense: people want homes, schools, and shops restored. Speed has costs, however. Rebuilding on the same vulnerable ground with the same methods can recreate the conditions for the next disaster. Planners who advocate building back better argue that recovery is a rare chance to improve, by moving structures from danger zones and using stronger designs. Residents, however, may fear that careful planning will delay their return or change their neighborhood beyond recognition. Successful recoveries appear to reconcile the two: they restore essential services quickly, while giving communities a voice in how much should be changed.
options: Moving Structures Out of Danger Zones
Residents Fearing Their Neighborhood Will Change
Quick Recovery Versus Safer Rebuilding
How Communities Cope with Disasters
quests.correctAnswer: Quick Recovery Versus Safer Rebuilding
quests.hint: The passage lays out two pressures. Which title includes both, and the way they are resolved?
quests.explanation: Coping with disasters is wider, moving structures is one planner's proposal, and residents' fears are one pressure. The passage reaches a conclusion about how successful recoveries balance speed with improvement.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title names the tension between speed and improvement and the reconciliation the last sentence describes.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Many languages have different words for 'you' depending on age, rank, or closeness, and choosing wrongly can offend. English dropped its formal form centuries ago, and speakers sometimes assume that English is therefore egalitarian. Politeness has not disappeared, though; it has moved into other devices: titles, tone, indirect requests, and even the choice of 'could' over 'can.' Linguists note that speakers who never use a formal pronoun still convey deference constantly. The difference between languages lies less in whether respect is expressed than in where the grammar places it. What seems like simplicity in one language may be the redistribution of complexity.
options: How Languages Place Politeness Differently
Speakers Choosing 'Could' Over 'Can'
English Losing Its Formal Pronoun
Differences Between English and Other Languages
quests.correctAnswer: How Languages Place Politeness Differently
quests.hint: The passage ends by saying what seems simple may be something else. What?
quests.explanation: Differences between English and other languages is wider, and 'could' versus 'can' and the lost pronoun are single points. The main claim is that respect is expressed in every language, only through different means.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title expresses the idea that all languages carry politeness, placed in different parts of the grammar and usage.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: When engines became more fuel-efficient, one might expect total fuel use to fall. Economists have observed that it often does not, because efficiency makes travel cheaper, and people travel more. The idea, known as the rebound effect or Jevons paradox, appears with lighting, computing, and heating. It does not mean that efficiency is pointless; savings still occur, though smaller than expected. It does mean that technical improvements alone rarely deliver promised reductions in resource use unless accompanied by limits or prices that keep total demand in check. Efficiency is a means; without something to restrain consumption, it may simply be spent.
options: Ways to Conserve Energy and Resources
Cheaper Travel Encouraging People to Travel More
The Rebound Effect: Efficiency That Gets Spent
Savings Occurring but Smaller Than Expected
quests.correctAnswer: The Rebound Effect: Efficiency That Gets Spent
quests.hint: Notice that the last sentence says efficiency 'may simply be spent.' What idea is that?
quests.explanation: Conservation methods is wider, cheaper travel is the main example, and smaller savings are a qualification. The passage's concept is the rebound effect and its implication for policy.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice names the effect the passage describes and captures its conclusion about efficiency without limits.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: A good title makes a promise and keeps it. It tells the reader roughly what to expect, without giving away everything, and it fits the text that follows. Titles fail in two opposite ways: too broad, they promise more than the text delivers; too narrow, they draw attention to one detail and ignore the rest. Less obvious is the third failure, a title that is accurate but points the reader in the wrong direction, stressing a minor topic instead of the main claim. Editors often write the title last, when they know what the piece is really about. Readers can use the same method: finish the passage, ask what the writer most wants understood, and only then test each candidate against the whole.
options: Role of Editors in Publishing
Titles That Are Too Broad or Too Narrow
Judging Titles Against the Whole Text
Writing the Title After the Piece Is Finished
quests.correctAnswer: Judging Titles Against the Whole Text
quests.hint: This passage is about the very skill you are practicing. What are its parts, and what does the last sentence ask you to do?
quests.explanation: Editors, the two kinds of scope failure, and writing the title last are all real points in the passage. The passage as a whole describes what a good title must do and how a reader can test it.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title covers the standard for a good title, the ways titles fail, and the method of testing a title against the whole passage.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: For years, I believed that reading well meant reading fast. I collected books the way others collect stamps and measured myself by numbers. Then, on a slow train journey, I brought only one book, an old novel with a plain cover, and I read it in small portions, looking out of the window between chapters. By the end I remembered more of that single book than of the previous twenty. I had not become a better reader by acquiring skill; I had become one by giving attention to something for long enough that it could reach me. Since then I read less, and I no longer count.
options: Ways to Choose Which Books to Read
Collecting Books Like Stamps
Reading One Novel During a Train Journey
Learning to Slow Down as a Reader
quests.correctAnswer: Learning to Slow Down as a Reader
quests.hint: The narrator changes a belief. Which title shows the whole change?
quests.explanation: Choosing books is a different topic, and the train journey and the collecting are two moments in the story. The passage traces a shift from valuing speed and numbers to valuing attention.
quests.whyThisTitle: It captures the writer's movement from reading fast to reading with sustained attention.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: It is often said that people no longer read carefully, and there is evidence to support the complaint: skimming has become common, attention is fragmented, and long texts are abandoned quickly. Yet the same period has produced an enormous appetite for long-form podcasts, serialized novels, and detailed explanations written by strangers for strangers. Perhaps the accurate description is not that people read less deeply but that they choose more selectively, giving their full attention to what earns it and skimming the rest. If so, the challenge for writers is not to shorten everything, but to make it clear early why a text deserves the effort of a careful reading.
options: Selective Attention Rather Than Declining Attention in Modern Reading
How Technology Is Changing Reading Habits
Skimming and Abandoning Long Texts
Rising Appetite for Podcasts and Serialized Fiction
quests.correctAnswer: Selective Attention Rather Than Declining Attention in Modern Reading
quests.hint: The passage starts with a complaint and then offers 'Perhaps.' Which title reflects the writer's own view?
quests.explanation: Technology's effect is wider, skimming is the complaint, and the appetite for long-form content is the counter-evidence. The passage puts both together and proposes that attention is selective rather than diminished.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title expresses the writer's proposal that readers give full attention selectively rather than simply attending less.
